title: The Small Blue Hour
premise: Lena Dunmore has spent thirty years tuning pianos and listening to the histories houses keep in their pipes and radiators, cataloguing the silences of her small coastal town in a notebook no one has ever seen. When a late-night radio program plays a song she knows was written by her brother Theo and never recorded—before he drowned in 1994—she realizes someone else survived that night and has been carrying the melody ever since. Returning to the shuttered seaside hotel where Theo died, Lena pieces together what really happened: her father's cover-up, a witness who became a recluse, and the role her own childhood silence played. In the end she chooses testimony over invisibility, playing the unfinished song aloud at the hotel's ruin and giving the town a truth it never asked for, accepting that justice outside the law costs her the careful anonymity she built her life on.
about_author: Rafael Eastwick is the pen name of a former piano technician who spent two decades tuning instruments in coastal towns along the Atlantic seaboard before turning to fiction. His work explores the quiet violence of small communities and the people who keep their secrets, and this is his third novel.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. We meet her in her ordered world: tuning pianos, reading houses through their radiators, keeping her notebook of silences. A routine job at the old Harrow house unsettles her when the pipes seem to 'remember' a storm. Emotional beat: the comfort of invisibility, with a hairline crack forming beneath it.

chapters.title: A Song With No Address
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Driving home at the blue hour, the radio plays a melody she knows intimately—Theo's unfinished composition, played on a battered upright. She pulls over, shaking. The announcer credits no composer. Emotional beat: vertigo; the past announcing itself in public.

chapters.title: What the Father Kept
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, with a memory chapter in Theo's voice from 1994. She searches her late father's effects and finds a pawn ticket and a torn photograph from the Meridian Hotel, where Theo drowned. Flashback shows the brothers' last summer. Emotional beat: grief sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Man Who Listens to Houses
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She tracks the radio signal to a part-time DJ, Elias Vann, who admits he recorded the song from a hermit living in the dunes near the ruined Meridian. Elias warns her the man, Oskar, trusts no one. Emotional beat: reluctant alliance; the first step out of hiding.

chapters.title: Return to the Meridian
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. She drives to the shuttered hotel where Theo died, hearing its decayed radiators like a dying choir. She finds evidence someone lives there—warm kettle, sheet music fragments. Emotional beat: dread and recognition; the house remembers her too.

chapters.title: Oskar
chapters.summary: Alternating Lena and Oskar POV. Oskar, the hotel's former caretaker's son, reveals he witnessed Theo's death: it was no accident. Lena's father paid him to disappear, and the song was Theo's gift to him the night before. Emotional beat: two keepers of silence recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Weight of a Witness
chapters.summary: Oskar's POV. His history unfolds—thirty years of guilt, of playing Theo's song to an empty ballroom, of the town's quiet decision to forget. Lena's father, it emerges, was protecting someone still alive and prominent. Emotional beat: the cost of silence compounding into something unforgivable.

chapters.title: The Name in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Lena's POV. Following the pawn ticket and hotel ledger, she confirms the other person present that night was her father's business partner, now the town's beloved patriarch, Judge Alden Marsh. Marsh's family begins quietly pressuring Lena to stop asking. Emotional beat: rising menace; the law itself is the wall.

chapters.title: The Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, climax. Marsh offers her hush money; she refuses. That evening, at the blue hour, she and Oskar open the Meridian's ballroom and she plays Theo's song aloud on the ruined piano while Elias broadcasts it live. The town listens. Emotional beat: testimony as act of love and defiance.

chapters.title: Everything Said at Last
chapters.summary: Lena's POV, resolution. An investigation reopens; Marsh's empire cracks; Oskar, no longer a hermit, plays the song's final movement with her. Lena writes the last page of her inventory and closes the notebook. Emotional beat: grief integrated, invisibility surrendered, identity claimed through voice.
